Guilty? Oh, Lord, yes. It eats at me lately. I just... I keep thinking I let the residents down. I have this bad habit of speaking too big, you know? Promising things before I actually sit down and check the money. 

Like last month, I told everyone at the board meeting we were going to get new paving for the visitor parking lot. The potholes out there are just awful. My niece, Sarah, she came to visit me for Easter, and she drives this little blue Honda Civic, sits real low to the ground. Well, she hit a pothole near the dumpsters and it knocked her hubcap right off! We spent twenty minutes looking for it in the bushes. The landscaping crew—oh, don't even get me started on them, they leave the clippings everywhere, just blow them right into the storm drains. Which is a code violation, by the way. I told the city inspector about it when he came out, but he just handed me a pamphlet. A pamphlet! What on earth am I supposed to do with a glossy trifold piece of paper? The city just doesn't care anymore, they really don't. It's all just red tape and people wanting to get off the clock by three-thirty. 

But, um... what was I saying? Oh, right, the paving. I promised everyone we'd fix it, and then I finally looked at the reserve accounts and realized we just don't have the funds for it. I just feel so terrible about it. Even though, I mean, nobody has actually come out and said I ruined anything. Not a single person has yelled at me or said a word about it. But I just sit there feeling like I completely failed them by opening my mouth before checking the bank.

Well, I suppose it's a bit of both, but really, I just... I just don't have the desire to do them anymore. Like, I haven't wanted to go to my dance class at all lately. I usually love that class. We do a bit of salsa, some ballroom. My instructor, Julian, he's from Colombia, and he has this incredible energy. He always wears these bright shirts, like neon pink and electric blue. I asked him where he buys them once, and he told me his sister makes them for him. Can you imagine having a sister who sews all your clothes? My sister, Brenda, she can barely sew a button on a shirt. She tried to hem a pair of slacks for my nephew's graduation, and one leg ended up two inches shorter than the other! He had to wear them anyway because the stores were all closed, and he looked ridiculous walking across the stage. 

And graduation ceremonies, oh, they drag on forever, don't they? They read every single name, and people bring air horns now. Air horns! Inside a gymnasium! It echoes so terribly, it just gives you a splitting headache. I think they ought to ban them entirely, but the school board says they can't police what people bring in their purses. Which is nonsense, they check bags at the baseball stadium all the time. 

But, oh, right, my activities. Yes, I just haven't wanted to go to dance, or even go look at the little art galleries downtown like I usually do. I haven't even been cooking my big Sunday dinners for the family. And those are the things that usually make me feel like myself, you know? I just... I don't care to do them right now.

Weight? Oh, well, I don't know if I've lost a significant amount, but my eating has definitely been off. Some days I just have my morning coffee and maybe a few bites of toast, and that carries me through the whole afternoon. I just don't have the stomach for a big meal. I buy those little loaves of bread from the bakery down the street—the one on Elm, not the one by the bank, the bank one always burns the crusts. The baker on Elm, Mr. Rossi, he makes the most wonderful sourdough. He told me the starter is fifty years old! Can you imagine? Fifty years of yeast. His father brought it over from Italy, or maybe it was his grandfather. They keep it in this special crock in the back. 

I used to bake bread when the kids were little. The whole house would smell like yeast and flour. It's such a comforting smell. But you know, flour gets everywhere. You find it on the cabinets, on the floor, on the dog... We had a golden retriever back then, Buster. Oh, he was a good boy, but he shed like you wouldn't believe. Clumps of fur rolling around like tumbleweeds in a western movie. I bought one of those fancy vacuum cleaners, the ones that cost as much as a small car, just to keep up with Buster's hair. The salesman came right to the door to demonstrate it. He poured dirt right on my nice rug! I nearly had a heart attack, but I'll be darned, that machine sucked it right up. 

But anyway, eating. Yes, I just haven't been eating right. Like I said, coffee and a few bites during the day, and then at night... I don't know, I just find myself picking at things. A tortilla here, some sweets there. But I'm not even really enjoying it. I just chew on it while I'm sitting there. So I suppose my weight might be down a little bit with all that, but I haven't really been keeping track.

The landscaping crew—oh, don't even get me started on them, they leave the clippings everywhere, just blow them right into the storm drains. Which is a code violation, by the way. I told the city inspector about it when he came out, but he just handed me a pamphlet. A pamphlet! What on earth am I supposed to do with a glossy trifold piece of paper? The city just doesn't care anymore, they really don't. It's all just red tape and people wanting to get off the clock by three-thirty. \n\nBut, um... what was I saying? Oh, right, the paving. I promised everyone we'd fix it, and then I finally looked at the reserve accounts and realized we just don't have the funds for it. I just feel so terrible about it. Even though, I mean, nobody has actually come out and said I ruined anything. Not a single person has yelled at me or said a word about it. But I just sit there feeling like I completely failed them by opening my mouth before checking the bank.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel your lack of interest in activities is more due to not enjoying them or not having the energy to participate?\n\nPatient: Well, I suppose it's a bit of both, but really, I just... I just don't have the desire to do them anymore. Like, I haven't wanted to go to my dance class at all lately. I usually love that class. We do a bit of salsa, some ballroom. My instructor, Julian, he's from Colombia, and he has this incredible energy. He always wears these bright shirts, like neon pink and electric blue. I asked him where he buys them once, and he told me his sister makes them for him. Can you imagine having a sister who sews all your clothes? My sister, Brenda, she can barely sew a button on a shirt. She tried to hem a pair of slacks for my nephew's graduation, and one leg ended up two inches shorter than the other! They read every single name, and people bring air horns now. Air horns! Inside a gymnasium! It echoes so terribly, it just gives you a splitting headache. Which is nonsense, they check bags at the baseball stadium all the time. \n\nBut, oh, right, my activities. Yes, I just haven't wanted to go to dance, or even go look at the little art galleries downtown like I usually do. I haven't even been cooking my big Sunday dinners for the family. I don't care to do them right now.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel your lack of interest in activities is getting worse over time?\n\nPatient: Well, worse... I suppose it's been pretty steady since it really hit me. This whole sharper change, you know, the energy dropping out from under me, my confidence just vanishing, and then this awful low, cloudy feeling settling in—it's been going on for about two weeks now. Right around the time my husband, Arthur, finally retired. \n\nHe was a claims adjuster for thirty-eight years. Thirty-eight years! And now he's just... home. All day. Every single day. Though I told him the leather was going to crack if he didn't condition it, and sure enough, there's a split right down the left armrest. He put a piece of duct tape over it! Duct tape on a Macy's chair! I told him it looks like we live in a fraternity house, but he just laughed and turned the television up. He watches those old Westerns, the ones in black and white where the horses always look like they're running in fast motion. \n\nAnd the volume! My instructor, Julian, he's from Colombia, and he has this incredible energy. He always wears these bright shirts, like neon pink and electric blue. I asked him where he buys them once, and he told me his sister makes them for him. Can you imagine having a sister who sews all your clothes? My sister, Brenda, she can barely sew a button on a shirt. She tried to hem a pair of slacks for my nephew's graduation, and one leg ended up two inches shorter than the other! He had to wear them anyway because the stores were all closed, and he looked ridiculous walking across the stage. \n\nAnd graduation ceremonies, oh, they drag on forever, don't they? They read every single name, and people bring air horns now. Air horns! Inside a gymnasium! It echoes so terribly, it just gives you a splitting headache. I think they ought to ban them entirely, but the school board says they can't police what people bring in their purses. Which is nonsense, they check bags at the baseball stadium all the time. \n\nBut, oh, right, my activities. Yes, I just haven't wanted to go to dance, or even go look at the little art galleries downtown like I usually do. I haven't even been cooking my big Sunday dinners for the family. And those are the things that usually make me feel like myself, you know? I just... I don't care to do them right now.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel your lack of interest in activities is getting worse over time?\n\nPatient: Well, worse... I suppose it's been pretty steady since it really hit me. This whole sharper change, you know, the energy dropping out from under me, my confidence just vanishing, and then this awful low, cloudy feeling settling in—it's been going on for about two weeks now. Right around the time my husband, Arthur, finally retired. \n\nHe was a claims adjuster for thirty-eight years. Thirty-eight years! And now he's just... home. All day. Every single day. He just sits in his recliner, the brown leather one we got at Macy's—well, it was on sale, but it's still a very nice chair. Though I told him the leather was going to crack if he didn't condition it, and sure enough, there's a split right down the left armrest. He put a piece of duct tape over it! Duct tape on a Macy's chair! I told him it looks like we live in a fraternity house, but he just laughed and turned the television up. He watches those old Westerns, the ones in black and white where the horses always look like they're running in fast motion. \n\nAnd the volume! He must be going deaf, I swear it rattles the good china in the dining room hutch. My mother gave me that china when we got married. It's Noritake, the Azalea pattern. You can't even find pieces for it anymore unless you scour those antique malls, and the people running those booths charge an arm and a leg for a single teacup. I saw one lady asking forty dollars for a saucer that had a chip right on the rim. A chip! I told her she ought to be ashamed of herself, but she just went right back to reading her paperback romance novel. \n\nBut, um, what was I saying? Oh, right. The last two weeks. Yes, ever since Arthur retired and has been home all day, that's when this low, cloudy feeling really took hold. It hasn't necessarily gotten worse since then, it just... it's just been sitting there on me for the last couple of weeks.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're depressed most of the day?\n\nPatient: Most of the day? Well, I suppose so, yes. From the minute I wake up, it just feels like this heavy blanket is over me. I usually wake up around six-thirty, even without an alarm. Arthur, on the other hand, he sleeps right through until nine now that he's retired. And he snores! Oh, it's like a freight train going through the bedroom. I bought him those little strips you put over your nose, the ones they advertise on the television with the little cartoon guy? I saw them at the pharmacy when I was picking up my face cream. \n\nThe pharmacist there, Brenda, she's such a sweet girl, but she's always looking so frazzled. She told me they cut her hours and she's trying to pay off her student loans. It's a crime what they charge for college these days, it really is. My nephew went to a state school and he's still paying it off, and he's thirty-two! He works in, oh, what is it... data entry? Something with computers. He sits in a cubicle all day. I couldn't do that, just staring at a screen. I need to be out talking to people, checking on the properties, making sure the landscaping is done right—though, like I said, they just blow the clippings everywhere. \n\nBut, oh, I'm sorry, what were we talking about? The depression? Yes, it's pretty much all day long. I just can't seem to shake it, no matter what I'm doing. It's just there, from morning till night.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you've lost interest in most things most of the time?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, most of the time, I'd say so. Like I mentioned before, I just haven't wanted to go to my dance class at all, or go look at the little art galleries downtown. And I haven't even been cooking my big Sunday dinners for the family. Those are the things that usually make me feel like myself, you know? But lately... nothing. \n\nAnd speaking of Sunday dinners, my sister Brenda—the one who ruined the slacks, you remember—she decided she was going to host last Sunday since I wasn't up to it. She made a pot roast. Or, well, she called it a pot roast. It was tough as shoe leather! I swear, you needed a chainsaw to get through it. And the carrots were mush. How do you burn the meat and turn the carrots to mush in the same pot? It defies logic. She bought the roast at that new supermarket on 5th Street, the one with the organic section that costs twice as much. I told her, you don't need organic beef if you're just going to cook it until it's gray. \n\nThe cashier there, though, a young boy named Tommy, he's very polite. He always helps me bag the groceries because my arthritis acts up. He told me he's saving up for a car. A used Honda, I think he said. Hondas run forever, you know. My first car was a Honda, a little red hatchback. I drove it all the way to Florida one summer with my girlfriends. We stopped at this roadside diner in Georgia, and they had the best pecan pie... \n\nBut anyway, what were you asking? Oh, right, losing interest. Yes, most of the time, I just don't have the drive to do the things I normally love. It's just all day, most days, nothing sounds appealing.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been feeling this way, exactly?\n\nPatient: Well, exactly... let's see. This latest stretch, the really heavy one, like I said, it started about two weeks ago, right when Arthur stopped working. But honestly, these depressed stretches... they've been coming back on and off for about a year now. \n\nA year ago, that was right around the time we had to replace the water heater in the basement. Oh, what a mess that was! It rusted out right at the bottom and flooded the whole utility room. Ruined three boxes of Christmas decorations. The good ornaments, too! The glass ones I bought when we went to that little Bavarian village tourist town up in the mountains. Leavenworth, I think it was called. They had this shop that sold nothing but nutcrackers. Hundreds of them! Some were as tall as I am. I bought a little one, a soldier with a red coat, but the paint started chipping off after just a few years. They don't make things like they used to, do they? Everything is just cheap plastic now. \n\nThe plumber who came to fix the water heater, he was a nice enough fellow, but he charged by the hour and took three coffee breaks! I watched him from the kitchen window. He just sat in his van, drinking out of a thermos and looking at his phone. I wanted to march out there and tell him I wasn't paying him to play games on his telephone, but Arthur said to just let it be. Arthur always says to let it be. That's his whole philosophy in life, which is probably why he's so content to just sit in that cracked leather chair all day. \n\nBut, oh, I'm wandering again, aren't I? I'm sorry. You asked how long. Yes, the off-and-on spells have been happening for about a year, but this current, really bad one is definitely tied to Arthur retiring two weeks ago.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost a significant amount of weight over the past year?\n\nPatient: Weight? Oh, well, I don't know if I've lost a significant amount, but my eating has definitely been off. Some days I just have my morning coffee and maybe a few bites of toast, and that carries me through the whole afternoon. I just don't have the stomach for a big meal. I buy those little loaves of bread from the bakery down the street—the one on Elm, not the one by the bank, the bank one always burns the crusts. The baker on Elm, Mr. Rossi, he makes the most wonderful sourdough. He told me the starter is fifty years old! Can you imagine? Fifty years of yeast. His father brought it over from Italy, or maybe it was his grandfather. They keep it in this special crock in the back. \n\nI used to bake bread when the kids were little. The whole house would smell like yeast and flour. It's such a comforting smell. But you know, flour gets everywhere. You find it on the cabinets, on the floor, on the dog... We had a golden retriever back then, Buster. Oh, he was a good boy, but he shed like you wouldn't believe. Clumps of fur rolling around like tumbleweeds in a western movie. I bought one of those fancy vacuum cleaners, the ones that cost as much as a small car, just to keep up with Buster's hair. The salesman came right to the door to demonstrate it. He poured dirt right on my nice rug! I nearly had a heart attack, but I'll be darned, that machine sucked it right up. \n\nBut anyway, eating. Yes, I just haven't been eating right. I just chew on it while I'm sitting there. So I suppose my weight might be down a little bit with all that, but I haven't really been keeping track.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel that your current depressive episode is mild or more severe?\n\nPatient: Well, mild or severe... I'd say it's on the milder side, really. I'm still getting to work, managing the properties and all. But I've definitely had to slow down. I've been asking my assistant, Carla, to double-check all the vendor details. Carla's a sweetheart, really. She just got engaged to a boy who works down at the hardware store. They're planning a spring wedding, hoping for an outdoor ceremony by the lake. I told her, you have to have a backup plan for rain in April. You just never know with spring weather. \n\nI remember my own wedding, it rained buckets! We had to move the whole reception inside the VFW hall at the last minute. The caterer was furious because the kitchen there was half the size of the one at the country club. He was a very high-strung man, wore this little white chef's hat that kept tipping to the side when he yelled. He made the most divine stuffed mushrooms, though. I tried to get the recipe from him for years, but he took it to his grave. \n\nBut, oh, what was I saying? Right, work. So I've had Carla checking things, and I've even had to put off a couple of board items because I just... I just don't trust my judgment right now, you know? It's like my brain is moving through molasses. So I guess it's mild since I'm still functioning, but it's definitely slowing me down.\n\nDoctor: Do you find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Pleasure... no, not really. That's actually been one of the hardest parts. I just haven't wanted to do the things that usually make me feel like myself. Like my dance class. I haven't been in weeks. It's a tap class for seniors, you know, at the community center. We wear these little black shoes with the metal taps on the bottom. Clickity-clack, clickity-clack! It's such a joyful sound. The instructor, Miss Debbie, she used to be a Rockette back in the seventies. She has legs up to her ears and still does high kicks! She showed us a picture of herself in the Radio City Christmas Spectacular once. Those costumes with the sequins... I always wondered how they washed them. You can't just throw sequins in the washing machine, they'd snag on everything. You probably have to hand wash them in the sink with Woolite. I use Woolite for all my delicate sweaters. \n\nBut anyway, I haven't been to dance. And I haven't even wanted to go look at the little art galleries downtown either. There's this one gallery that always has the most beautiful watercolor landscapes, but I just can't muster the energy to care. And Sunday dinners... I haven't cooked Sunday food for my family since this whole thing started. I usually make a big roast or a lasagna, but the thought of standing in the kitchen for hours... I just can't do it. My grandson, little Tommy, he loves my lasagna. He calls it \"Nana's magic pasta.\" He just started first grade and he's already reading chapter books! He's so smart, gets it from my side of the family, definitely not Arthur's. Arthur's brother still reads with his finger under the words. \n\nBut yes, to answer your question, I just haven't had the desire to do my dance class, or the galleries, or the cooking... the things I usually love.\n\nDoctor: Would you say your current depressive episode is interfering with your daily life to a significant degree?\n\nPatient: Well, I wouldn't say it's completely stopping me in my tracks, but it's definitely getting in the way. Like I mentioned before, I'm still getting myself to work, managing the properties, but I've had to slow down so much. I'm just not making decisions the way I usually do. I've been having Carla double-check all those vendor details. Oh, speaking of vendors, the new landscaping company we hired for the Oakwood property? They planted the wrong color impatiens! I specifically asked for the soft pink ones, you know, the ones that look so lovely against the brick in the spring. But they put in these garish bright magenta ones. Magenta! It clashes terribly with the red brick. I tried to tell the foreman, a nice young man named Luis, but I think he just didn't understand why it mattered. \n\nColor coordination is so important. My mother always taught me that. She used to make all my clothes when I was a little girl. Beautiful little dresses with matching hair ribbons. She had this old Singer sewing machine, the kind with the foot pedal. She'd sit there for hours, just pumping that pedal. You don't see craftsmanship like that anymore. Now everything is just bought off the rack, made of that awful polyester that makes you sweat. \n\nBut anyway, work. Yes, it's interfering. I've even had to put off a couple of board items because I just... I really don't trust my own judgment right now. I just feel like I might make a mistake, like with the impatiens, though that wasn't my mistake, but you know what I mean. So I'm still functioning, but it's taking a lot more effort than it should.\n\nDoctor: Would you describe your current feelings of depression as mild, moderate, or severe?\n\nPatient: Well, I suppose I'd call it mild, if I had to put a word on it. I mean, I'm still getting up and going to work every day, managing the properties. But it's just... I've really had to slow down on making decisions. I've been having Carla double-check all the vendor details, like I said. She's been so helpful, bless her heart. She actually brought in these wonderful blueberry muffins yesterday. Her aunt makes them from scratch. Her aunt lives over in Shelbyville, in one of those beautiful old Victorian houses with the wrap-around porches. I always wanted a wrap-around porch. You could sit out there in the evening with a glass of iced tea and just watch the fireflies. Arthur always said they were too much upkeep, the wood rots and you have to paint them every five years. He was always so practical. Sometimes too practical, if you ask me. He wouldn't even let me paint the front door red. Said it looked too \"flashy.\" \n\nBut yes, work. I've even had to put off a couple of board items lately. I just... I don't trust my judgment right now. It takes so much effort just to think things through. So, mild, I guess, since I'm still doing things, but it's certainly not my normal."
